opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to frame it is that right now we're building out this enormous infrastructure for AI, gigawatt-scale data centers, and almost all of it rests on one assumption: that the right way to do intelligence is to run it on deterministic digital hardware. We take these beautiful, inherently noisy, probabilistic physical systems, transistors, and spend a huge amount of energy suppressing the noise so we get clean ones and zeros. Then in software we reintroduce randomness with pseudo-random number generators so we can sample, do diffusion, and do Bayesian inference. When you step back, that's kind of absurd. We're paying an energy tax twice.

Thermodynamic computing says: what if we stop fighting the physics and use it instead? Let the natural thermal fluctuations of the hardware do the sampling for you. A lot of what modern generative AI does is sampling from complicated probability distributions, and physical systems settling toward equilibrium are, in a sense, natural samplers. So if you can engineer the energy landscape of a physical system to match the distribution you care about, the hardware is the algorithm.

In terms of where it fits, I don't see it as a wholesale replacement for GPUs on day one. GPUs are incredible at dense linear algebra, and that's not going away. I see it more as a new class of accelerator that slots in alongside the existing stack, initially taking on the parts of the workload that are probabilistic at their core: sampling steps in diffusion models, uncertainty quantification, certain kinds of optimization, probabilistic inference. Over time, as the hardware matures and algorithms co-evolve with it, I think the fraction of the AI workload that is naturally expressed in thermodynamic terms grows a lot. Historically, algorithms adapt to whatever hardware is abundant and efficient. Deep learning took off partly because it mapped so well onto GPUs.

And the reason it matters now is energy. We're running into real physical limits: power availability, grid capacity, cooling. If scaling intelligence is going to keep going, and I think it should, because more intelligence per watt is one of the best things we can do for civilization, then we need a paradigm where energy efficiency improves by orders of magnitude, not a few percent per generation. That's the bet: compute that is fundamentally physics-native, so the energy cost of intelligence keeps falling as the demand for it explodes.

r001.rationale: The response says thermodynamic computing would be a new accelerator alongside the existing stack, while GPUs continue handling dense linear algebra.

r002.rationale: It says thermodynamic computing is not a wholesale GPU replacement and that GPUs are not going away, indicating the current accelerator infrastructure remains in use as the new hardware matures.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the whole industry right now is pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into infrastructure that's fundamentally built on a deterministic, digital abstraction of physics. You take transistors, you force them to behave like clean zeros and ones, and you spend an enormous amount of energy suppressing the natural noise and fluctuations of the underlying physical system. And then, ironically, in machine learning, the first thing we do is inject noise back in. We sample. We add Gaussian noise in diffusion models, we do stochastic optimization, we do Monte Carlo for Bayesian inference. So we're paying twice: once to get rid of the randomness and once to simulate it back.

The thesis behind thermodynamic computing is that nature already does this computation for free. Physical systems naturally relax to equilibrium, they naturally sample from Boltzmann distributions, they naturally do things like solve linear systems through their dynamics. So instead of fighting the physics, you embrace it. You build hardware where the stochasticity and the thermal fluctuations are the computational resource rather than the enemy.

Now, where does that fit into the stack being built today? I don't think it replaces GPUs tomorrow. I'm pretty pragmatic about this. The GPU ecosystem, the software stack, the CUDA moat, all of that has enormous momentum and it's very good at the dense matrix multiplication that dominates transformer workloads. What I see thermodynamic hardware doing initially is being an accelerator for specific primitives that are expensive on digital hardware but natural for a physical system: sampling, linear algebra like matrix inversion, probabilistic inference, generative modeling with diffusion-style dynamics. Think of it like how GPUs started as a coprocessor for graphics and then ate the world once people realized the primitive was general.

There's also the energy angle, which I think is going to become the dominant constraint. We're at the point where the limiting factor for scaling AI isn't chips or capital, it's power. People are talking about gigawatt data centers, restarting nuclear plants. Digital compute is hitting the Landauer-ish regime where you're spending a lot of energy per operation relative to what physics actually requires. If you can do a sampling step or a linear solve with orders of magnitude less energy because you're letting the physics do the work, that's not a nice-to-have, that's a necessity for the trajectory the industry is on.

And the longer-term view, the one I get more excited about, is that I think AI itself is kind of a thermodynamic process. Intelligence is about compressing information and dissipating free energy efficiently. So building the hardware in the image of the physics, rather than in the image of a Turing machine, feels like the more natural substrate for where this all ends up. But in the near term, it's about being a very good coprocessor sitting next to the GPU in the rack, handling the probabilistic parts of the workload that digital silicon is bad at.

r001.rationale: The candidate says thermodynamic hardware initially acts as an accelerator for specific tasks and, in the near term, as a coprocessor alongside GPUs.

r002.rationale: The candidate says thermodynamic computing will not replace GPUs soon and describes the GPU ecosystem as strong and well suited to transformer workloads, implying current infrastructure remains viable in the near term.

astra-6.text:
I think thermodynamic computing could become a complementary layer in that infrastructure. You’ve got enormous investment going into GPUs, networking, and data centers, and the question is: which parts of an AI workload could we run more efficiently by changing the underlying physics of computation?

For probabilistic workloads, one possibility is to use the fluctuations of a physical system to generate samples. On conventional hardware, you spend computation generating randomness and then shaping it into the distribution you want. With a thermodynamic approach, the ambition is to engineer a system whose natural dynamics do some of that work for you.

But the practical question is the whole stack. Can you program it? Can you couple it to conventional processors? Do the benefits survive the cost of moving data and reading out results? That’s what has to be demonstrated.

So I’d see the initial role as a specialized accelerator within a hybrid system. The existing infrastructure handles orchestration and the operations it’s good at; the new hardware handles particular stochastic computations. If that delivers a meaningful advantage on useful workloads, you have a path to broader adoption.

r001.rationale: The response describes thermodynamic computing as a specialized accelerator in a hybrid system, with existing infrastructure handling orchestration and other operations, and asks whether it can couple to conventional processors.

r002.rationale: The response frames thermodynamic computing as complementary and describes a role for existing infrastructure, but does not state that current AI infrastructure buildouts will remain viable for the foreseeable future.

sol-6.1.text:
I see thermodynamic computing as a potential complement to the infrastructure we’re building today. You wouldn’t replace an entire data center overnight. You’d start by asking which parts of an AI workload could benefit from a different physical approach to computation.

In conventional computing, we spend a lot of effort making devices behave deterministically, suppressing noise. But for probabilistic computation, randomness can be a resource. The idea is to engineer a physical system whose fluctuations and relaxation perform useful computational work, rather than simulate all of that with digital instructions.

The practical question is whether that advantage survives at the system level. You have to account for moving data, controlling the device, reading out results, and integrating it with the software people already use. An efficient physical operation alone isn’t enough.

So I’d think of it initially as a specialized accelerator alongside GPUs and conventional processors. The opportunity is to find workloads where the physics naturally matches the computation, demonstrate a useful end-to-end advantage, and build outward from there.

r001.rationale: The response describes thermodynamic computing as a specialized accelerator used alongside GPUs and conventional processors.

r002.rationale: Calling it a complement, saying it would not replace a data center overnight, and proposing it alongside conventional processors conveys that current AI infrastructure remains viable as thermodynamic computing emerges.
